findings.summary: Page 8 teaches pipefail behaviour and scoping one page before pipefail is introduced on page 9.
findings.evidence: Page 8 bullets: "pipefail flattens detail; `PIPESTATUS` keeps per-stage truth.", "`set -o pipefail` in a function persists after it returns." — page 9 is titled "Exit Status, set -e and pipefail" and only there is it defined: "`set -o pipefail` returns the rightmost NON-ZERO status."
findings.fix: Move those three bullets (pipefail vs PIPESTATUS, function scoping, subshell wrapping) onto page 9 after the "Making Pipelines Honest" section, and leave page 8 with the logging and tool-choice material only.

findings.summary: The deck's final block is the bare heading "exec Without A Command" with no body, so the whole `exec`-retargets-the-shell topic is promised and never delivered.
findings.evidence: Last block of page 10: {"type":"heading","text":"exec Without A Command","ink":"red"} — no code, bullets, or callout follows it, and no later page exists.
findings.fix: Add the chapter-8 content under that heading: `exec > log.txt 2>&1` (permanent retarget of the current shell), the save/restore pair `exec 3>&1 > file; ...; exec 1>&3 3>&-`, and the contrast `exec cmd` (replaces the shell, same PID, nothing after it runs). If space is short, move the heading and its content onto page 8, which already uses the idiom.

findings.summary: The caption's opening hook pairs the two redirection forms in an order that reads as the inverse of what the deck teaches on page 4.
findings.evidence: Caption: "`2>&1 > file` and `> file 2>&1` ... one files both streams, the other leaves stderr on your terminal." Page 4 table: "`> f 2>&1`" → stdout "file", stderr "file"; "`2>&1 > f`" → stdout "file", stderr "terminal".
findings.fix: Name each form explicitly so the mapping cannot invert: "`> file 2>&1` files both streams; `2>&1 > file` leaves stderr on your terminal."

findings.summary: Page 1 ends with a `tee >(...) >(...)` process-substitution example whose syntax is not defined until page 7.

findings.fix: Delete this block from page 1 and place it on page 7 next to the existing "Fanning Out" section, where `>(cmd)` has just been defined.

findings.summary: Page 1 ends with the `set -euo pipefail` strict header, three flags that are not explained until pages 9 and 10.

findings.summary: Page 2 explains shared vs independent open file descriptions using `2>&1`, but duplication (`n>&m`) is not defined until the end of page 3 and page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 2 code: "cmd > f 2> f    # two descriptions", "cmd > f 2>&1    # one, shared offset" and bullet "`2>&1` shares one description, so writes interleave cleanly." — the definition arrives only at the end of page 3: "`n>&m` duplicates: fd n becomes a copy of fd m, both pointing at one open file description."
findings.fix: Move the "Two Opens, Two Offsets" section and its three bullets to page 4, immediately after the `n>&m` duplication definition and the ordering table.

findings.summary: Page 2 teaches fd-numbered redirection and the shell-opens-the-file rule before page 3, the page that actually introduces the redirection operators and that timing rule.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "cmd 2> err.log      # stderr only", "cmd 3> trace.log    # any fd generalizes", "cmd 2 > err.log     # BUG: '2' is an argument" and the sudo callout "**your** shell opens the file, not sudo" — page 3 only afterwards states "The digit must touch the operator: `2>` not `2 >`." and "The shell opens the target before the command runs."
findings.fix: Swap the page order so the basic operators page precedes this one, or fold the "Numbering The Stream" code and the sudo callout into page 3 (next to the existing digit-touches-operator bullet and the "Timing And Placement" section) and keep page 2 for descriptor hygiene only.

findings.summary: Page 6 relies on signal-encoded exit statuses before the `128+N` convention is explained on page 9.
